caption:
Who discovered the Ajanta Caves?

On 28 April 1819 a British officer, John Smith of the 28th Cavalry, was hunting tigers in the gorge of the Waghur river when a local shepherd boy showed him the entrance to Cave 10. Smith fetched villagers with axes, spears, torches and drums to cut back the tangled jungle. Inside he saw painted ceilings, then monastic halls. He scratched his name and the date across a painting of a bodhisattva. He was standing on a five-foot pile of rubble, so the graffiti now sits above an adult's eye level.

Thirty rock-cut halls are carved into a 75-metre wall of rock: monasteries and worship halls, made in two phases between the 2nd century BCE and about 480 CE. Each cave began as a narrow tunnel at roof level, widened downwards and outwards. Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 hold the largest surviving body of ancient Indian wall painting, done in dry fresco on dry plaster.

They were never lost. Medieval Chinese Buddhist travellers mention them, and the 17th-century Ain-i-Akbari lists twenty-four rock-cut cave temples here.

Still open: the dates. Walter Spink puts nearly all the later work in 460u2013480 CE; the Archaeological Survey of India still dates the second phase of painting to the 5thu20136th centuries. And the pale figures in Cave 1, once read as a Persian embassy, are now thought simply to show people from far-away lands.

Images: Fergusson's 1845 lithograph of Cave 10, the 1880 Fergusson and Burgess section of Cave 19, a 1958 encyclopaedia photograph of the Cave 19 facade, and fresco photographs by Sweekar Bhushan Pamulaparthy and Daderot.
